PASSO 1: lembre do português. Para dizer: STEP 1: good news — this tense is English "had + past participle": "I had left", "she had done". Spanish builds it exactly the same way: «había salido», «había hecho». STEP 2: the catch: English "have" is both possession and the auxiliary; Spanish splits them. Possession is «tener», but the auxiliary is ALWAYS «haber». So "I had a car" is «Tenía un coche», but "I had eaten" is «Había comido» — never «tenía comido». STEP 3: the auxiliary is «haber» in the imperfecto: «había, habías, había, habíamos, habíais, habían». Every form has an accent on the «í». STEP 4: then comes the participle: -ar verbs take «-ado» (hablado), -er and -ir verbs take «-ido» (comido, vivido). When the stem ends in a strong vowel (a, e, o), «-ido» takes an accent: «leído, oído, traído, creído, caído». STEP 5: the irregular participles are the same ones you already use with «he»: hecho, dicho, visto, puesto, escrito, abierto, vuelto, roto, muerto, cubierto, resuelto — and their compounds: «deshecho, descrito, devuelto, descubierto». Watch out: Spanish never adds «-ido» to these («escribido», «hacido» don't exist), just as English doesn't say "writed". STEP 6: with «haber», the participle NEVER agrees: «Ella había salido», «Ellas habían salido». STEP 7: the auxiliary and the participle stay together — nothing goes in between. English says "I had ALREADY left", "I had NEVER seen", "I had seen IT"; Spanish moves those words outside: «Ya había salido», «Nunca había visto», «Lo había visto». STEP 8: careful: «había» is also the past of «hay» («había mucha gente» = there were a lot of people). If a participle follows, it's the auxiliary.

STEP 1: think of two past events. One is the event you're telling («cuando llegué»). The other had already happened BEFORE it («el tren salió»). STEP 2: the more recent event, your reference point, takes the indefinido or the imperfecto: «Cuando llegué…». The older event takes the pluscuamperfecto: «…el tren ya había salido». STEP 3: so the full sentence is «Cuando llegué, el tren ya había salido» (When I arrived, the train had already left). First the train left, then I arrived. STEP 4: words that help you spot the order: «ya, todavía no, aún no, nunca, antes, hasta entonces, al + infinitive, cuando». STEP 5: «ya» and «todavía no» usually go before the auxiliary: «ya había salido», «todavía no habían llegado». STEP 6: use the pluscuamperfecto to explain a cause: «Llegó tarde porque había perdido el autobús» (He was late because he had missed the bus). STEP 7: and to say what you had never done up to a point: «Hasta aquel viaje, nunca había estado en Sevilla». STEP 8: if the events are told in the order they happened, you don't need it: «Llegué, cené y me acosté». STEP 9: don't confuse it with the pretérito perfecto: «No he comido» looks from the present; «No había comido» looks from a moment in the past.

Negação, pronomes e perguntas no pluscua: Negation, pronouns and questions in the pluscuamperfecto
PASSO 1: a negação vem antes de tudo: «N: STEP 1: negation comes first: «No había terminado». STEP 2: object and reflexive pronouns go before the auxiliary: «Lo había visto» (I had seen it), «No lo había visto», «Se había dormido» (he had fallen asleep). English puts "it" at the end; Spanish puts «lo» in front of «había». STEP 3: to ask, change the intonation and, if you like, put the subject after: «¿Habías estado antes en Madrid?» (Had you been to Madrid before?), «¿Ya habían llegado tus padres?». STEP 4: short answers: «Sí, ya había estado», «No, todavía no había llegado» — no "Yes, I had" with the auxiliary alone. STEP 5: a very useful pattern: «Ya había + participle + cuando + indefinido»: «Ya había anochecido cuando salimos» (It had already got dark when we left). STEP 6: to explain the reason for a state, use «porque» + pluscuamperfecto: «Estaba cansada porque no había dormido bien». STEP 7: «ya» and «todavía no» help your listener see that there are two moments.

When she got to the station, the train had already left. She asked at the information desk and they told her the next one left at eleven. While she waited, she called her friend Elena, who was waiting for her in Valencia, and explained what had happened. Elena didn't get angry; on the contrary, she had already booked a table for lunch at three and there was plenty of time. Marta finally arrived at half past twelve. Until then, she had never been so happy to see a friend. They had lunch together and, after coffee, Elena showed her the photos of the harbour, where she had walked on her own the day before.
